statement: In one double-blind laboratory study of 8 adults who were already using cocaine and alcohol together, adding alcohol to repeated cocaine doses was associated with a higher heart rate, roughly 13% to 15% more cocaine in the blood over the session, and cocaethylene, a substance the body makes only when both drugs are present. In 8-hour inpatient sessions, with four nasal cocaine doses 30 minutes apart (1 mg per kg each) and oral alcohol dosed to hold the blood level near 100 mg/dL (study conditions, not amounts to use), heart rate was higher with the combination than with cocaine alone (p = .002; about 84 against 74 beats a minute averaged over the session, an editors' calculation from the printed areas under the curve). Cocaine exposure was higher with alcohol (p = .035), and cocaethylene, never found with either drug alone, cleared more slowly than cocaine (half-life 156 against 85 minutes). People rated feeling good more highly with the combination than with cocaine alone (p = .04) but did not rate any high significantly higher (p = .09), and blood pressure did not differ detectably from cocaine alone; blood alcohol was lower with cocaine (99 against 118 mg/dL at the one time point reported). A narrative review of 14 small laboratory studies, which includes this one, describes second-hand up to 30% more blood cocaine, cocaethylene only with both drugs, and heart-rate rises that were additive with a trend towards greater than additive; it also describes one 6-person study in which alcohol came 30 minutes after cocaine and blood cocaine did not rise. The review adds that no retrospective study it covers shows unequivocally that the combination harms the heart more, and that one emergency-room study of over 1,000 patients found no more cardiovascular problems in people positive for both drugs than for one. The study had 8 people, gave cocaine by the nose to people who usually smoked it, and counted p below .05 one-tailed as significant across 15 measures without correction, so the heart-rate result is the sturdiest and the cocaine-exposure and feel-good results would not reach .05 on a two-tailed test (an editors' calculation). It reports no heart events or rhythm findings, cannot say whether the heart-rate rise came from the extra cocaine or from cocaethylene, and cannot show what happens outside a ward.
plain: What happens when cocaine and alcohol are taken together? In one careful hospital study of 8 adults who already used both, heart rate was higher with both than with cocaine alone, there was roughly 13% to 15% more cocaine in the blood, and the body made cocaethylene, a substance that forms only when both drugs are present and that stays in the blood longer than cocaine. People said they felt better with both than with cocaine alone, but their rating of any high did not clearly differ. A review of other small laboratory studies describes similar findings, and also says that emergency-room studies do not clearly show more heart problems with both drugs than with one. With only 8 people, just the heart-rate result was clear, and the study did not report on heart attacks or rhythm problems. It was done on a ward, with cocaine by the nose, not in everyday life.
population: Eight non-treatment-seeking adults (4 men, 4 women; mean age 33) who were already using cocaine and alcohol together and met DSM-IV criteria for cocaine dependence and alcohol abuse, tested as hospital inpatients; the review adds 14 prospective laboratory studies of 6 to 34 people each (13 with 12 or fewer), this one among them, described second-hand
exposure: Four intranasal cocaine doses (1 mg per kg every 30 minutes) with oral alcohol (1 g per kg after the first cocaine dose and 120 mg per kg at 60 minutes, aimed at a blood level near 100 mg/dL), given on a ward; study conditions only
comparator: The same people on other days with the same cocaine and a placebo drink, and with placebo cocaine (lactose) and the same alcohol; there was no session with both drugs replaced by placebo, and they knew the three conditions would occur, in random order
outcome: Heart rate and blood pressure over 8 hours, ratings of any high, feeling good and other effects, and blood levels of cocaine, cocaethylene and alcohol
magnitude: McCance-Katz et al. (1998), combination against cocaine alone: heart rate p = .002 (areas under the curve over 480 minutes 40,289 (SEM 940) against 35,658 (647); editors' calculation, averages of about 83.9 against 74.3 beats per minute; alcohol alone 34,778 (933), about 72.5). Blood pressure: no significant difference from cocaine alone; the combination was higher than alcohol alone (systolic p = .008, diastolic p = .003). Cocaine: peak 893 (SEM 114) against 754 (114) ng/mL; area under the curve 153,562 (19,489) against 135,371 (19,892) ng x min/mL, described as about 15% greater (editors' calculation from the printed means: 13.4%), p = .035; half-life 85 against 83 minutes. Cocaethylene, only with the combination: half-life 156 (15.3) minutes, longer than cocaine (p = .001); peak 114 (18) ng/mL at 180 minutes; its area under the curve is 0.20 of cocaine's. Ratings: feel good higher than with cocaine alone (p = .04, peak at 120 minutes); any high p = .09; rush, sleepy, paranoid, crash, sad or depressed and desire for cocaine not significantly different (no values printed). Blood alcohol lower with the combination (p = .008, data not shown; 99 (SE 7) against 118 (10) mg/dL 30 minutes after the second alcohol dose). The paper counts p below .05 one-tailed as significant across 15 measures without correction; doubling the p values (editors' calculation) gives about .07 for cocaine exposure and .08 for feel good. Pennings et al. (2002), second-hand: blood cocaine up to 30% higher when cocaine came with or after alcohol (5 studies, this one among them); cocaethylene only with both drugs (6 studies); blood alcohol unchanged in 1 study and about 10% lower, not significantly, in 4; heart rate additive with a trend towards greater than additive; one 6-person study with alcohol 30 minutes after cocaine: heart-rate rises additive and no rise in blood cocaine; in over 1,000 emergency-room screens, no more cardiovascular problems in people positive for both drugs than for one.

evidence.locator: Methods and Materials > Subjects, 1st paragraph; Procedures, 1st paragraph; Study Design, 1st paragraph
evidence.extracted: Eight non-treatment-seeking volunteers (4 men, 4 women; mean age 33) who were already using cocaine and alcohol together, with cocaine as the preferred drug, and who met DSM-IV criteria for cocaine dependence and alcohol abuse, stayed as inpatients and were told to abstain from drugs and alcohol for 3 days before admission. Double-blind, within-person, three 480-minute sessions in random order, no more often than every 2 days: four doses of intranasal cocaine (1 mg/kg every 30 minutes) with oral alcohol (1 g/kg after the first cocaine dose and 120 mg/kg at 60 minutes, calculated to hold plasma alcohol near 100 mg/dL); the same cocaine with placebo alcohol; lactose in place of cocaine with the same alcohol (no session had both drugs replaced by placebo). Participants knew the three possible conditions; doses were set by lean body weight. The usual intake printed for the group (cocaine 5 g a week with a standard error of 7; 14 standard drinks a week with a standard error of 50) cannot be right for 8 people.

evidence.locator: Results, 1st paragraph (p. 252); Figure 1 and its legend (p. 253)
evidence.extracted: Heart rate was significantly higher after each dose with cocaine plus alcohol than with cocaine alone (p = .002) or alcohol alone (p = .002). Printed areas under the curve over 480 minutes (in the key inside the Figure 1 image, so not in the text layer): 40,289 (SEM 940) for the combination, 35,658 (647) for cocaine alone, 34,778 (933) for alcohol alone. Systolic and diastolic pressure rose with both cocaine conditions, with no significant difference between cocaine plus alcohol and cocaine alone; the combination raised systolic (p = .008) and diastolic (p = .003) pressure above alcohol alone. Read approximately from the figure (an image): the combination peaked near 95 beats per minute at 120 minutes and cocaine alone near 82. Editors' calculation (area divided by 480 minutes): averages of about 83.9, 74.3 and 72.5 beats per minute.

evidence.locator: Results, 4th paragraph (starts p. 252, continues p. 253); Table 1 (p. 255); Discussion, 4th paragraph (starts p. 256; the area ratio is on p. 256)
evidence.extracted: Cocaine: peak 893 (SEM 114) ng/mL at 113 minutes with alcohol against 754 (114) at 116 minutes without (the peak difference is not tested); area under the curve 153,562 (19,489) against 135,371 (19,892) ng x min/mL, described as about 15% greater with alcohol, p = .035; half-life 85 and 83 minutes. Cocaethylene, formed only with the combination: half-life 156 (SEM 15.3) minutes, longer than cocaine (p = .001); peak 114 (18) ng/mL at 180 minutes, about 22% of the cocaine concentration then; area under the curve 31,050 (4,706), 0.20 (0.01) of the cocaine area; ratio to cocaine about 0.13 at 120 minutes and 0.40 at 360 minutes. Editors' calculation from the printed means: the cocaine area is 13.4% greater with alcohol.

evidence.locator: Results, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs; Figures 2 and 3 (pp. 254-255, images)
evidence.extracted: Rating of any high greater with the combination than with cocaine alone but short of significance (p = .09); the cocaine-high rating did not differ from cocaine alone (and was greater than with alcohol alone, p = .002); feel good greater than with cocaine alone (p = .04), peaking at 120 minutes, with a slight reduction in feel good with cocaine alone over the sessions. Rush, sleepy, paranoid, crash, sad or depressed and desire for cocaine showed no statistically significant findings (no values printed).

Plasma alcohol was lower with the combination than with alcohol alone (p = .008; data not shown in the paper); 90 minutes into the session (30 minutes after the second alcohol dose) it averaged 99 (SE 7) mg/dL with cocaine and 118 (10) without, against a target near 100. The authors suggest that swallowed cocaine slows alcohol absorption by narrowing blood vessels in the stomach.

evidence.locator: Methods and Materials > Data Analysis, 1st paragraph (p. 252); Discussion, 4th paragraph (pp. 256-257) and 5th, 6th, 7th and 9th paragraphs (p. 257)
evidence.extracted: All 15 measures were compared as areas under the curve in a repeated-measures analysis, with planned comparisons of the combination against each drug alone, one comparison per measure; every test with p below .05 (one tailed) was counted as significant, with no correction, justified by directional hypotheses from the authors' earlier study. The authors suggest cocaethylene may matter more for heart effects late in the session (4th paragraph), and say the findings point to an increased risk of organ ischaemia, infarction and arrhythmia (5th); the paper reports no heart events or rhythm findings, and no test separates an effect of cocaethylene from the rise in cocaine. Participants were chosen because they already used both drugs (6th paragraph); the authors say it is unclear whether people who use both drugs have a premorbid vulnerability to psychiatric disorders or whether the combination is more toxic to the central nervous system than cocaine alone (7th); they list the intranasal route as a limit, since smoked or injected cocaine might give larger effects (9th).

evidence.locator: Methods > Inclusion and exclusion, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (p. 774); Table 1 (p. 775)
evidence.extracted: The review (a narrative review: databases and years are stated, but no counts of records found or excluded) lists in Table 1 prospective laboratory studies with 6 to 34 people each; the study above is one of them. Cocaine was given intranasally or intravenously and never smoked, and the placebo in most studies was a 4 mg or 5 mg dose of cocaine (Table 1 footnote). Only a few studies had at least two active doses of each drug, which the review says is needed to speak of synergy, so it uses the word 'potentiation' loosely. Editors' count of the Table 1 rows: 14 studies, 13 of them with 12 or fewer people.

evidence.locator: Results > Prospective research > Heart rate, 1st paragraph (p. 774); Blood levels and toxicokinetics, 1st paragraph (p. 776); Cocaethylene production, 1st paragraph (p. 777)
evidence.extracted: As described by the review: when cocaine was given at the same time as or after alcohol, most studies showed a trend towards greater-than-additive heart-rate effects but did not support synergy; blood cocaine was up to 30% higher with the combination in five studies (the study above among them); blood alcohol was unchanged in one study and about 10% lower, not significantly, in four; cocaethylene formed only when both drugs were given, never with either alone (six studies), and also when alcohol followed cocaine by 30 minutes. The review's text and Table 1 describe the study above as showing greater-than-additive increases in heart rate and in 'any high'; that study compared the combination only with each drug alone, had no session with both drugs replaced by placebo, and found any high short of significance (p = .09).

evidence.locator: Results > Prospective research > Heart rate, 2nd paragraph (pp. 774, 776); Blood levels and toxicokinetics, 2nd paragraph (p. 776)
evidence.extracted: Order of dosing: in a 6-person study (Perez-Reyes, 1994) in which cocaine was given 30 minutes before alcohol, heart-rate rises were additive, blood cocaine was not higher than with cocaine alone and the rating of high did not change, unlike earlier studies in which alcohol came first; cocaethylene formed in both orders. The review calls alcohol before cocaine the more common order, without citing a source.

evidence.locator: Retrospective studies > Cocaethylene and toxicity, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs (pp. 778-779)
evidence.extracted: As described by the review: whether cocaethylene or the higher cocaine level explains the heart-rate rise is controversial, and talk of greater cardiotoxicity may be premature, since no retrospective study shows unequivocally that the combination leads to more of it; one study of over 1,000 emergency-room toxicology screens found no more cardiovascular problems in people positive for both drugs than for one, and another found less chest pain but more back and limb pain with the combination, without an alcohol-only group. A single case report of an 18-year-old who died suddenly of cardiotoxicity after cocaine, alcohol and cannabis is set against the larger study.

risk_of_bias.note: Double-blind, within-person, random order, with objectively measured heart rate and drug levels; but participants knew the three possible conditions and alcohol is hard to mask, every test was counted as significant at .05 one-tailed across 15 measures without correction, and several results are printed without values (clinician ratings, six rating items, blood alcohol); the study card rates the risk of bias high overall.

inconsistency.note: Only one primary study was read; the review describes other laboratory studies pointing the same way for blood cocaine and cocaethylene and a trend for heart rate, as the claim says, and its emergency-room data show no clear excess of heart problems, which the claim also says.

indirectness.note: None as worded: the claim is limited to what was measured in these sessions and says that other routes, other settings and heart events are not covered.

imprecision.note: Eight people and no intervals for the contrasts; the cocaine-exposure and feel-good results (p = .035 and .04, about .07 and .08 doubled) are fragile, and only the heart-rate result (p = .002) is large relative to its spread.

grade.reasoning: A double-blind, within-person laboratory study with random order of conditions starts high (METHODS 6.3). Risk of bias -1: unmasked alcohol, one-tailed uncorrected tests across 15 measures and results printed without values; the study card rates the risk of bias high overall. Imprecision -2: 8 people, no intervals, and fragile results for cocaine exposure and feel good. Inconsistency 0 and indirectness 0 as worded. Certainty very low. Status: single study; the narrative review that includes this study describes similar findings second-hand, is not appraised and overlaps this study, so it is not counted as replication. The claim does not say that the effects are more than additive (the study compared the combination with each drug alone and had no session with both drugs replaced by placebo, although the review's table lists it as greater than additive), and it does not say that the combination raises the chance of a heart attack or a rhythm problem, which none of the sources read measured.

verification.flag_note: One laboratory study read in full (McCance-Katz et al. 1998) plus the narrative review that lists it (Pennings et al. 2002); the other laboratory studies in the review (Farre 1993 and 1997, Perez-Reyes and Jeffcoat 1992, Perez-Reyes 1994, McCance-Katz 1993, Higgins 1993) were not read and have no reference records here; reading two of them would allow status replicated. Smoked or injected cocaine, heavy repeated use and heart outcomes are not covered by any source read.
